title: IELTS Speaking Complete Guide
subtitle: Band 7+ strategy: marking criteria, fluency, vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, Parts 1, 2 and 3 - from the nextED Speaking book

chapters.title: How to Use This Book
blocks: Of the four IELTS modules, Speaking is the one that test-takers in our country fear the most. The reason is simple - in Reading, Listening and Writing you sit and work on your own, but in Speaking you have to sit face to face with an unfamiliar examiner and speak in English for 11 to 14 minutes. Even after twelve years of studying English at school and college, most of us have almost no practice in actually speaking it. As a result, a student who scores 7.5 in Reading gets stuck at 5.5 in Speaking.

This book has one purpose - to make the Speaking test **predictable** for you. If you know in advance what will happen in the test, what the examiner will be looking for, what kinds of questions will come up and which answers get which band, then preparation takes the place of fear.
The Four Parts of This Book
The structure of the Speaking test, how the examiner awards marks, the elements of good speaking, band descriptors, linking words, pronunciation, and strategies for test day.
Read it all once first. Later, before each practice session, go back over the relevant section.
Part 1 strategies, plus questions and model answers for 30+ common topics.
Practise 2-3 topics aloud every day. Don't memorise - put in your own information when you speak.
How to organise the 2 minutes of the cue card, a method for taking notes, and a framework for answering the abstract questions in Part 3.
Practise each framework on at least 5 different topics.
Cue cards by theme, each with notes, a model talk and possible Part 3 questions.
Practise with a timer. Record yourself and listen back.

**A word of warning:** The model answers in this book are not meant to be memorised. Examiners conduct hundreds of tests every day; they spot a memorised answer within the first two sentences. When the examiner detects a memorised answer, they change the question, and your band goes down. Read the model answers to learn **structure**, **vocabulary** and **ideas** - then build your own answers using facts from your own life.

chapters.title: The Structure of the IELTS Speaking Test
blocks: The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with a certified examiner (even in the computer-delivered test, it is with a real examiner, via video/in another room). The whole conversation is **recorded**. The Speaking test is the same for both Academic and General Training candidates. It takes 11 to 14 minutes in total and is divided into three parts.
The examiner introduces themselves and checks your name and ID. Then they ask 3-4 short questions each on 3 familiar topics (e.g. home, work/study, hobbies, food, weather).
Whether you can speak naturally, quickly and accurately about familiar topics.

You are given a card with a topic and 3-4 points. You have 1 minute to make notes. Then you must speak for 1-2 minutes without stopping. At the end, the examiner may ask 1-2 short follow-up questions.
The ability to speak at length, continuously and in an organised way.

Questions related to the Part 2 topic, but broader, social or abstract. For example, if you had to talk about a gift in Part 2, Part 3 might include: "Why do people give gifts?", "Has gift-giving changed in your country?"
Whether you have the language to give opinions, make comparisons, explain reasons and speculate about the future.
A Few Things to Get Clear First

**A longer or shorter test has nothing to do with your score.** Some people's test ends in 11 minutes, others' in 14. The examiner follows a fixed script; when time is up, they may stop you mid-sentence. This is not a bad sign.
**You can't tell anything from the examiner's facial expression.** They are trained to stay neutral. If they didn't smile, that doesn't mean you are doing badly.

**It is your language that is assessed, not the content of your answer.** The examiner does not check whether your opinion is "correct" or whether your story is true. They listen to how effectively you can say it in English.
**The same examiner marks all three parts**, and the score is based on the whole test - if you do poorly in one part, you have a chance to make up for it.

chapters.title: What Exactly the Examiner Looks For: The Four Criteria
blocks: IELTS Speaking is marked on four criteria. Each one gets its own band (0–9), and then the average of the four gives your Speaking band. The four carry **equal weight** - in other words, if you are weak in pronunciation, no matter how well you do in grammar, you cannot make up for the loss.
How well you can speak at a natural pace without unnecessary pauses, and whether what you say is logically organised and connected.
How wide and accurate your vocabulary is; whether you can say the same thing in different words; whether you can use idiomatic and less common words.
How many kinds of sentence structure you use (range), and how error-free they are (accuracy).
How easily your pronunciation can be understood by the listener; whether your word stress, sentence rhythm and intonation are natural.
The next four chapters discuss each criterion one by one. Before that, let's use a short question and answer to see how the four work together.
**Examiner:** Do you prefer to shop online or in physical stores?
✗ **Answer 1:** Online. Because online is easy. I can buy from home. Physical store is far.

FC: Every sentence stands alone, with no connection. LR: 'easy', 'far'- very basic words. GRA: only simple sentences, an article error ('Physical store' → 'A physical store'/'Physical stores'). This is a Band 5 answer.

**Answer 2:** To be honest, I've shifted almost entirely to online shopping over the last couple of years, mainly because it saves me the hassle of dealing with traffic. Having said that, for things like shoes, I still prefer going to a physical store, since I want to try them on before I pay.

FC: 'To be honest', 'mainly because', 'Having said that', 'since'- the answer flows. LR: 'shifted', 'hassle', 'try them on'- natural and precise. GRA: present perfect ('I've shifted'), participle clause ('Having said that'), reason clause. This is a Band 7+ answer.

Notice - the second answer is **not much longer, it is much better organised**. This is the core message of this book: your band goes up not by saying more, but by raising the quality of what you say.

chapters.title: Understanding Band Scores: 5 to 8
blocks: The band descriptors are the list the examiner uses to award marks. They are a public document, but the language is quite technical. Below, I have written in plain language exactly what the examiner listens for in each of the four criteria at each band. Record yourself and compare it with this list - you will be able to see for yourself where you stand.
Band 5 - "Can keep talking, but it's a struggle"

Can speak, but to keep going they repeat the same things again and again, speak slowly, and pause while trying to correct their own mistakes. Uses some linking words (and, but, because), but the same ones keep coming back. Fine with easy questions; with slightly more complex questions, fluency breaks down.
Has enough words to get by on familiar topics, but gets stuck on unfamiliar ones. Attempts to paraphrase, but often gets it wrong.
Simple sentences are mostly correct. Attempts complex sentences, but most contain errors, and the errors sometimes get in the way of the meaning.
Between Band 4 and 6: some words are clear, others take effort for the listener to understand. Little or no stress and intonation.
Band 6 - "Everything is understood, but there are errors"

Willing and able to speak at length, but sometimes pauses, repeats or self-corrects - which breaks the coherence. Uses linking words, but not always correctly (e.g. starting a sentence with 'moreover' and then moving on to a different topic).
Has enough vocabulary to speak at length on any topic, but word choice is sometimes inappropriate. Generally paraphrases successfully.
Uses both simple and complex sentences. There are errors in complex sentences, but they rarely get in the way of the meaning.
Some use of stress, intonation, etc., but not consistently. Understandable overall, though mispronunciation of some words/sounds sometimes reduces clarity.

Can speak at length without noticeable effort. Sometimes pauses or self-corrects - but to think about the content, not to search for language. Uses linking words and discourse markers (well, actually, the thing is...) naturally.

Uses vocabulary **flexibly** across a range of topics. Has some less common and idiomatic words and an awareness of collocation (make a decision, heavy traffic, highly recommend), though there are occasional errors. Paraphrases effectively.
Uses a variety of complex structures flexibly. Most sentences are error-free; some errors remain.
All the features of Band 6 and some of the features of Band 8. Easy to understand throughout; the influence of the first language may be heard, but it does not affect understanding.
Band 8 - "Fluent, almost like a native speaker"
Fluent; rarely pauses or repeats, and when they do pause, it is to think about the topic. Develops topics logically and easily.
A wide vocabulary for expressing precise meaning on any topic. Uses less common and idiomatic words skilfully; errors are rare. Paraphrases easily whenever needed.
Uses a wide variety of structures flexibly. Most sentences are error-free; only occasional errors or inconsistencies.
Uses a wide range of pronunciation features. Easy to understand throughout; the influence of the first language is almost non-existent.
What Does Moving from 6 to 7 Really Mean?

Most test-takers in Bangladesh get stuck at 6 or 6.5. If you put the two lists above side by side, you will see that to move up to 7, what you need is not so much to learn something new as to **reduce your old mistakes**:
What needs to happen at Band 7
Pauses to search for language ("I... I think... the... umm...")
Pauses only to think of ideas; even when pausing, the language is natural ("Well, let me think... I'd say...")
Uses linking words, but mechanically ("Firstly... Secondly... Moreover...")
Linking is natural and varied ("The main reason is... On top of that... Mind you,...")
Words are correct but ordinary ("good", "bad", "very big")
Stress on key words, rise and fall in sentences

**Remember:** Band 7 does not mean perfect. Even at Band 7 there are some errors and occasional pauses. People who try to be perfect and think through every sentence as they speak lose their fluency and drop to 6. The goal is not perfection - it is to be **comfortable and reasonably accurate**.

chapters.title: Fluency & Coherence: Flow, Not Speed
blocks: Many people think being fluent means speaking fast. So in the exam room they try to speak as fast as possible, and as a result their pronunciation becomes slurred, their grammar falls apart and the examiner has to keep listening very carefully. Think of it the other way round - does a good speaker speak fast? No, they speak **at a natural pace, without stopping, without slurring**. Fluency is **flow** - the words come one after another in such a way that the listener never has to wait.
Fluency breaks down because of three things:
**Hesitation** - pausing to search for a word or structure. ("My hobby is... is... umm... playing... the...")
**Repetition** - saying the same word or phrase over and over to buy time to think. ("I like, I like, I like cricket because, because...")
**Self-correction** - noticing a mistake and going back to fix it. ("She go... she goes... she went to...")
How to Pause When You Need To

Pausing is not forbidden. Native speakers pause too. The difference is **how** they pause. A silent pause ("...") or a pause filled with "umm/aaa" damages fluency; but if you pause with an English filler phrase, it sounds like a natural part of conversation, and you can think during that time.
The question is difficult and you need time to think
That's an interesting question. / I've never really thought about that, but... / Let me think for a second.
A little time before you start your answer
Well, / Actually, / To be honest, / I'd say... / In my case,
...how should I put it... / ...what's the word... / ...I mean...
You need to correct what you said
...or rather, / ...I mean, / ...actually, what I meant was...
I'm not entirely sure, but I'd guess... / I don't know much about that, but from what I've seen...

**Caution:** A filler phrase is an umbrella - open it when it rains, not in the sunshine. If you start every answer with "That's an interesting question", the examiner will realise it is a trick you've been taught. Use one about once every 3-4 answers, and vary the phrases.
What should you do if you make a mistake? Two rules:
If the mistake **changes the meaning** (e.g. you meant to say "I didn't like it" but said "I did like it"), correct it - briefly: "...sorry, I mean I didn't like it."

If the mistake is **a small grammar error** (article, -s, tense), **don't go back**. The examiner has heard the error anyway; if you go back and correct it, they will hear the error + hesitation - two losses. Keep going.

Fluency is about whether your speech keeps going; coherence is about whether it is **going somewhere**. Many students speak non-stop, but at the end the examiner can't tell what the answer to the question was. There is a simple structure for a coherent answer that works everywhere, from Part 1 to Part 3:

**The Core Answer Structure: A.R.E (Answer – Reason – Example)**
**A - Answer:** Answer the question directly in your very first sentence.

**R - Reason:** Why? One or two reasons.

**E - Example:** A concrete example or detail.

In Part 3 a fourth step is added - finishing with an opposing side or a condition (explained in detail in Part C).

**Q:** Do you think it's important to learn to cook?
**A (Answer):** Definitely, I think it's one of those basic life skills everyone should have.
**R (Reason):** For one thing, it's much cheaper than eating out, and you also have full control over what goes into your food.
**E (Example):** When I moved into a hostel for university, I couldn't even boil an egg properly, and I ended up spending a fortune on street food for the first few months.

A.R.E is the central strategy of this book (and the app) - it works everywhere from Part 1 to Part 3. For Part 1 there are two more, lighter strategies as well (**Direct Answer + Extension** and **L.D.F**), which are discussed in Part B. If you keep these three patterns in mind, the problem of "what else can I say?" almost disappears.
Linking Words: Which One for Which Job

Linking words, or discourse markers, are the words that create relationships between your sentences. Without them, your speech sounds like a list; with them, it sounds like an argument. Below they are grouped by function. For Speaking, the **conversational** forms in the right-hand column are more natural; the formal forms in the left-hand column belong to Writing - if you use them too much in Speaking, you will sound like you are reciting an essay.
In my opinion, I believe that
I'd say, Personally, To be honest, If you ask me, I reckon
mainly because, the main reason is, that's why, the thing is
On top of that, Also, Plus, Another thing is, What's more
For example, Like, Take... for example, Say,
But, Having said that, Mind you, Then again, On the other hand
So, That means, which is why, and because of that
First of all, Then, After that, Eventually, In the end
Actually, In fact, Especially, What really matters is
If, As long as, Depending on, It depends whether
So overall, All in all, At the end of the day, Basically
Let's look at a Part 3 answer to see how linking words turn **a list into an argument**.

✗ **Q:** Should smartphones be allowed in school classrooms?
No. Students get distracted. They use social media. Teachers cannot control. Some students use it for learning. Schools should have rules.
Five sentences, five islands. Which is the reason, which is the exception, which is the conclusion - it's left to the listener to work out.

I'd say no, at least not without strict rules, mainly because phones are a huge distraction. The thing is, the moment a lesson gets a bit boring, students drift off to social media, and teachers simply can't keep an eye on thirty screens at once. Having said that, phones can be useful for things like looking up a word or recording a lecture, so I think the sensible approach is to allow them only when the teacher asks for them. At the end of the day, it's about control, not a total ban.
The same ideas, but now the listener knows which is the main opinion, which is the reason, which is the exception and which is the conclusion.

**The danger of overuse:** One sign of Band 6 is using "too many" linking words. If you start every sentence with "Moreover" or "Furthermore", the examiner realises you have memorised a list. The rule: use a linking word only when you really need to show a relationship between two ideas.

chapters.title: Lexical Resource: The Right Word in the Right Place
blocks: Lexical resource does not mean "difficult words". The examiner looks for three things: (1) whether you have the **right** word for what you want to say, (2) whether you can say things in different ways instead of repeating the same word, and (3) whether your words come in **pairs** (collocations) the way native speakers use them.

In the speech of Bangladeshi test-takers, you hear a few "all-purpose" words most often: good, bad, nice, big, very, thing, a lot of. They are not wrong, but they tell the examiner nothing. Using different words in their place to suit the situation raises your LR band.
(food) delicious, mouth-watering  |  (work) rewarding, fulfilling  |  (people) considerate, easy-going  |  (experience) memorable, worthwhile  |  (method) effective, practical
(experience) frustrating, disappointing  |  (weather) miserable, unbearable  |  (habit) harmful, unhealthy  |  (condition) run-down, poorly maintained
very tired → exhausted; very happy → delighted, over the moon; very cold → freezing; very crowded → packed; very expensive → pricey, extortionate; very interesting → fascinating
(city) sprawling, densely populated  |  (problem) major, serious  |  (change) dramatic, significant  |  (house) spacious
plenty of, a wide range of, countless, a great deal of (uncountable), loads of (informal)
be fond of, be keen on, be into, enjoy, can't get enough of, have a soft spot for
2. Paraphrase: Saying the Same Thing Differently

Handing the examiner's question words straight back (echoing) is a sign of Band 6. If you change the key word of the question into your own words, you show LR and at the same time get a natural way to start your answer.

**Q:** Is it important for children to play outside?
**Echo (weak):** Yes, it is important for children to play outside because...
**Paraphrase (strong):** Absolutely - I think getting kids out in the open air is essential, and honestly it's becoming rarer and rarer in cities like mine...
Even within one answer, if the same word keeps coming up, change it:

**Repetition:** My city is a busy city. The city has many people. I like my city.
**Varied:** My hometown is a pretty hectic place. It's densely populated, but I've grown quite attached to it over the years.

Many sentences that are grammatically correct but sound "unnatural" are the result of translating directly from Bangla. Native speakers don't say "do a mistake", they say "make a mistake". Some widely used collocations that are useful in Speaking:
do a mistake, do a decision
make a mistake, make a decision
take a rest for long time
take a break, have a rest
open the TV / close the light
turn on the TV / switch off the light
a good chance, a golden opportunity
spend time studying, devote time to studying
the price is low / high; it's cheap / expensive
fast food is not healthy for health
fast food is bad for your health / unhealthy
4. Idiomatic Language: How Much, and How

The Band 7 descriptor mentions "some idiomatic vocabulary". This does not mean proverbs and sayings ("Every cloud has a silver lining") - those sound artificial in Speaking. It means the phrases that are natural in native speakers' everyday speech:
I'm really into photography these days.
My brother's a bit of a night owl.
My English isn't perfect, but I get by.
It's hard to keep up with all the new apps.
I'm not a big fan of horror films.
I usually eat breakfast on the go.
I need to hit the books this weekend.
I go to the cinema once in a blue moon.
it's not my cup of tea
Reality shows aren't really my cup of tea.
I was over the moon when I got the job.
Learning to cook pays off in the long run.
Many families struggle to make ends meet.
**Rule:** No more than 1 idiomatic phrase per answer, and only one that you have used many times before. Using an idiom in the wrong place lowers your LR; it doesn't raise it.

chapters.title: Grammatical Range & Accuracy
blocks: GRA has two parts: **range** (how many kinds of structure) and **accuracy** (how error-free). You need a balance between the two. Someone who only uses simple sentences gets stuck at 6 because of range, even if their accuracy is good. Someone who makes mistakes trying to make every sentence complex shows range but loses accuracy.

**The practical rule:** One error-free simple sentence is better than one complex sentence full of errors. But for Band 7, simple sentences alone are not enough. So the strategy is - **master 4-5 complex structures really well**, and use those same ones again and again. You don't need to know every structure.
The 6 Structures That Are Most Useful in Speaking

I usually walk to work, **since** the office is only ten minutes away.
**As** I grew up in a village, I'm quite used to a quiet lifestyle.

**Although** I enjoy cricket, I hardly ever get time to watch a full match.
**Even though** it's expensive, I think a good laptop is worth the money.

My grandmother, **who** is nearly eighty, still cooks for the whole family every Friday.
The area **where** I live has changed a lot in the last decade.

**If** I have a free weekend, I usually visit my parents. (general habit)
**If** I had more time, I'**d** definitely learn to play the guitar. (imagination - very useful in Part 3)
**If** I **had known** the exam would be this hard, I **would have** started earlier. (regret about the past)

Life in the city is **far more hectic than** it used to be.
Online courses are **not as effective as** face-to-face classes, in my experience.
That was probably **the most rewarding** thing I've ever done.

I **would imagine that** most people prefer working from home.
It's **likely that** paper books will become a niche product.
Governments **should** probably invest more in public transport.
People **tend to** spend more when they shop online.
Tense: Which One When in Speaking
I work as a pharmacist. I usually get up at six.
Temporary actions happening right now / around this time
I'm currently preparing for a job exam.
Specific past events (the story in Part 2)
Last year we went to Sylhet for a week.
Experiences that are still relevant, "how long"
I've lived here for six years. I've never been abroad.
It was raining heavily when we arrived.
Past habits that no longer happen
I used to cycle to school every day.
I'm going to apply for a master's next year.
The 10 Most Common Mistakes Made by Bangla Speakers
These come directly from Bangla grammar, so they don't sound wrong to our ears. But to the examiner's ear, every one of them is obvious.
'agree' is a verb, not an adjective.
'cousin brother' does not exist in English.
My sister, he is a doctor.
My sister is a doctor. She...
In Bangla, the pronoun 'se' has no gender; in English, he/she must be correct.
I am living in Dhaka since 2015.
I have been living in Dhaka since 2015.
Yesterday I went to the market.
With a past time marker, use the past tense; an article is needed before 'market'.
She has a lot of information.
I will discuss about the topic.
discuss, enter, reach, marry - no preposition follows these.
One of my friend told me.
One of my friends told me.
Despite of the rain, we went.
Despite the rain, we went. / In spite of the rain...

chapters.title: Pronunciation: Clarity, Not Accent
blocks: "My accent is Bangladeshi, so I'll get a low score in pronunciation" - this is not true. IELTS does not require any particular accent (British, American, Australian). The Pronunciation criterion measures only one thing: **how easily the listener understands you**. Even the Band 8 descriptor says a first-language accent may be present, as long as it does not affect understanding. So the goal is not to change your accent - the goal is to be clear.
To be clear, you need to work on four things: (1) certain specific sounds, (2) word stress, (3) sentence stress and rhythm, (4) intonation.
1. Sounds That Are Difficult for Bangla Speakers

In Bangla, both are close to the Bangla 'bh'/'o' sounds. Make sure 'very' doesn't become 'bhery', and 'we' doesn't become 've'. For /v/, the upper teeth touch the lower lip; for /w/, the lips are rounded and the teeth don't touch.
vine – wine, vest – west, vet – wet
'sea' and 'she' merge into one. Make sure 'Sun' doesn't become 'shun'.
sip – ship, sell – shell, sock – shock
Make sure 'zoo' doesn't become 'joo'. /z/ is like /s/, just with vibration in the throat.
zip – jip, zest – jest, prize – bridge
Make sure 'think' doesn't become 'tink' or 'thhink'. Place the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth and let the air out.
three – tree, thin – tin, then – den
Make sure 'fan' doesn't become 'phan'. For /f/, the lips don't close; the teeth touch the lip.
fan – pan, fill – pill, coffee – copy
Consonants at the end of words
In Bangla we often drop the final sound: 'card' → 'car', 'first' → 'firs'. Pronounce -ed and -s endings clearly - they carry grammar too.
work – worked, plan – planned, book – books
'ship' is short, 'sheep' is long. 'live' and 'leave' are different.
sit – seat, full – fool, bit – beat
2. Word Stress: Which Syllable Gets the Emphasis

In English, every word of more than one syllable has stress on one syllable. If you stress the wrong syllable, the listener may not recognise the word even if the sounds are correct. Some commonly mispronounced words:
Correct stress (stress on the capitalised part)

English is a "stress-timed" language - in a sentence, the **meaning-carrying words** (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) are said louder and longer, while **function words** (a, the, of, to, and, is) are said quickly and short. Bangla speakers say every word with equal stress, so their English sounds flat and mechanical.
I **WENT** to the **MARket** with my **SISter** to **BUY** some **VEGetables**.
Stress falls on the capitalised parts; 'to the', 'with my', 'some' are said quickly. Said this way, the same sentence sounds much more natural.
Changing the stress also changes the meaning - this is useful in Part 3 for strengthening an opinion:

**I** didn't say she took the money. (someone else said it)
I didn't say **she** took the money. (someone else took it)
I didn't say she **took** the money. (maybe she borrowed it)
4. Intonation: The Rise and Fall of Your Voice
**Lists:** The tone rises on every item except the last, and falls at the end. "I like cricket ↗, football ↗, and badminton ↘."
**Yes/No questions:** The tone rises at the end. "Do you like it ↗?"
**Wh-questions and statements:** The tone falls at the end. "Where do you live ↘."
**Showing interest:** "It was interesting" said in a flat tone sounds bored; raising the tone on 'interesting' shows you are genuinely interested.

**The most effective practice:** Shadowing. Take a 30-second section of an English podcast or interview. First, listen. Then speak along with the audio, with exactly the same stress and tone, at the same speed. 10 minutes a day for 4 weeks makes a visible difference to your pronunciation band.

chapters.title: Test Day: From Start to Finish
blocks: **"Warm up" in English.** In the hour before the test, don't speak in Bangla. Talk in English - to yourself, to a friend or on the phone. When your mouth and brain are in English "mode", the stiffness of the first two minutes goes away.
**Clothing:** There are no rules, but wear something normal, formal or smart-casual. The reason is not your score - it's your own confidence. Wear whatever makes you feel "ready".
**ID:** Bring the same passport/ID you used for registration. Without it, you cannot take the test.
**While waiting:** Don't try to find out from other candidates "what questions came up". It only increases nervousness, and everyone gets different questions anyway.
Entering the Room and the First Minute
Knock lightly on the door and say "May I come in?" - when the examiner says yes, go in, close the door, smile a little and say "Good morning/afternoon".
Remain standing until you are asked to sit. When you hear "Please have a seat", say "Thank you" and sit down.
The examiner will first start the recording and state their name, the date and the centre - this is part of the script; there is nothing you need to do.
Then: "Can you tell me your full name, please?" → your full name. "What shall I call you?" → the name you are comfortable being called. "Can I see your identification, please?" → hand over your ID.
You don't need to say anything extra in this part. It isn't marked - but this is where your first impression is formed. Clear, calm, smiling.

**Keep eye contact.** If you talk while looking at the table, the wall or your own hands, you sound nervous - and even if you are doing well, the lack of confidence shows. Look at the examiner's face rather than directly into their eyes; that's easier.
**Posture:** Sit up straight, back against the chair, hands in your lap or on the table. Jiggling your legs or twirling a pen only makes you feel more nervous.
**Speak at a normal volume, clearly.** The test is recorded; if you ask for re-marking later, that same recording is what will be listened to. Speaking very quietly hurts you in both places.

**If the examiner stops you, stop.** This is part of the script; it is nothing against you. If you are stopped in the middle of saying "...and that's why - ", say "Sure" and move on to the next question.

**If you don't understand a question:** "Sorry, could you repeat that, please?" - asking for a repeat once is completely normal. In Part 3, if a question is complex, you can check your understanding by saying "Do you mean ...?". But asking for repeats again and again on easy Part 1 questions makes your listening seem weak.
**Don't ask the examiner questions** ("What do you think?"). They won't answer; this is a one-way interview.
At the End of the Test

When you hear "Thank you, that's the end of the speaking test.", say "Thank you very much, have a good day" and get up. Don't ask how you did - the examiner can't tell you. Stand up, straighten the chair, and leave calmly.

chapters.title: 10 Speaking Tips
blocks: This chapter is a summary of the whole of Part A - ten working rules, arranged in the same order as the "Speaking Tips" section of the app. Each tip covers: why it matters, where in this book it is explained in detail, and one practice you can start today.

Pronunciation is one of the four criteria, which means it is 25% of your score. It doesn't change in a week, but 10 minutes a day makes a clear difference in four weeks. **Where:** The Pronunciation chapter - difficult sounds, word stress, sentence stress, intonation. **Practice:** Every day, say one pair from the list of difficult sounds (e.g. vest–west) 20 times, and one sentence 5 times aloud with the correct stress.

"Yes." "No." "Sometimes." - a one-word answer gives the examiner nothing to mark. Give at least one reason and one detail in every answer. **Where:** The A.R.E structure in the Fluency & Coherence chapter; the three Part 1 strategies in Part B. **Practice:** Take any Part 1 question and answer it within these limits - no fewer than 2 sentences, no more than 4 - and record it.

In Part 2 you have to speak for 2 minutes without stopping; without a structure, you run out of things to say in 40 seconds. If you know in advance a fixed order that follows the points on the card - what, when/where, why, feelings - you can fill 2 minutes on any topic. **Where:** Part C - the one minute of note-taking and the structure of the talk. **Practice:** Take a cue card from Part D and speak for 2 minutes with a timer; if you stop before 1 minute 30 seconds, do it again.

"Advanced" doesn't mean difficult, it means **precise** - not "good" but "rewarding"; not "very tired" but "exhausted". But the word has to come out as if it is your own, not forced in. A big word in the wrong place lowers your LR. **Where:** The Lexical Resource chapter - precise words, paraphrase, collocation. **Practice:** Listen to one of your own recorded answers, mark every 'very/good/bad/thing', put in alternatives and say it again.

In Part 3 the questions are not about you - they are about society, the future, causes and effects. There is no "correct" answer here; there is opinion + reason + example + the other side. For someone who knows this pattern, no question is unfamiliar. **Where:** Part C - types of Part 3 questions and the framework; the speculation structures in the Grammar chapter. **Practice:** Every day, pick one social issue (traffic, online learning, tourism) and speak about it from two sides for 30 seconds each.

Our mistakes are not random - the same ten or twelve mistakes that come from Bangla grammar keep coming back (I am agree, cousin brother, he/she, since + present). Once you catch these, your accuracy jumps in one go. **Where:** The "10 common mistakes made by Bangla speakers" list in the Grammar chapter. **Practice:** Read the ten correct sentences from the list aloud once a day, until the mistake sounds "wrong" to your ear.

Nervousness doesn't take away your language - it takes away your access to it. The cure is preparation and familiarity: knowing the format, knowing the script for the first minute, and knowing what to say when you need to pause. **Where:** The "Test Day" chapter; the list of filler phrases in the Fluency chapter. **Practice:** Get a friend to play the examiner and do a full 12-minute mock test - at least three times. By the third time, your fear will be cut in half.

The Band 7 descriptor mentions "some idiomatic vocabulary" - but not proverbs; everyday phrases (be into, get by, once in a blue moon). The rule: no more than one per answer, and only one you have used many times. **Where:** The list of idiomatic language in the Lexical Resource chapter. **Practice:** Take 3 phrases from the list each week and use each one in 3 sentences about your own life.

Shadowing - speaking along with a native speaker's audio at the same speed, stress and tone - builds fluency, pronunciation and natural phrasing all at once. It is the practice with the highest return in this book. **Where:** The Pronunciation chapter. **Practice:** A 30-second section of a podcast/interview: listen once, shadow it 3 times, 10 minutes a day.

There are hundreds of Speaking topics, but only 20-25 categories (work, education, environment, technology, health...). If you have 10-15 of your own words and collocations ready in advance for each category, the words will come even for unfamiliar questions. **Where:** The words worth underlining in the model answers for each topic in Part B; the vocabulary box of the cue cards in Part D. **Practice:** From each topic in Part B, copy 5 words/phrases into your own notebook and use them in your own sentences.

chapters.title: What Part 1 Is and Why It Matters
blocks: Part 1 is the first 4-5 minutes of the test. After checking your identity, the examiner chooses three topics - the first is almost always about your **work/study** or your **hometown/home**, and the other two can be any everyday subject (food, weather, sport, music, technology, etc.). Each topic has 3-4 short questions. The questions are **about you** - your habits, likes and experiences. There are no abstract or social questions here; those come in Part 3.
Many people take Part 1 lightly - "they're easy questions, I'll just say something". That's a mistake. Part 1 matters for three reasons:
**First impression.** The examiner forms an idea of you in the first two minutes. To change that idea later, you have to do a lot better.

**There are no excuses here.** If you get stuck on a difficult question in Part 3, the examiner understands that the topic is hard. But if you get stuck on "What do you do in your free time?", they assume you don't have basic fluency.
**This is your warm-up.** If Part 1 goes well, you go into Part 2 relaxed. If it goes badly, your nervousness grows and stays with you for the whole test.
How long should an answer be?

The most practical rule for Part 1: **2 to 4 sentences**. If you answer in one word or one sentence, you aren't giving the examiner a chance to hear your language. On the other hand, if you speak for 1 minute on a single Part 1 question, the examiner will stop you - and they will have less time to ask the next questions in their script. Answer + reason + one detail - that's the right size.

✗ **Q:** Do you often use public transport?
**Too short:** Yes, every day.

✗ **Too long:** Yes, I use public transport every day. I take the bus in the morning at 8 o'clock. The bus is number 27. It goes from my area to Motijheel. It takes one hour. Sometimes it takes one and a half hours. There is a lot of traffic. I don't like the traffic. Many people are on the bus. Sometimes I have to stand. When I stand it is difficult. After that I reach my office...
Long, but all simple sentences with no linking, and the examiner will stop you after 30 seconds.
**The right size:** Yes, pretty much every day, actually. I take the bus to work since it's by far the cheapest option, although the traffic on my route can be a nightmare during rush hour.
Every Part 1 question fits one of three patterns. If you can recognise the pattern as soon as you hear the question, your answer organises itself.

**Strategy 1 - Direct Answer + Extension (2 steps)**
**When:** simple, factual questions - your name, your work, your home, how long, who you live with. No reason is asked for here; one extra piece of information is enough.

**Step 1 - Direct Answer:** answer directly, in one sentence.

**Step 2 - Extension:** one related detail - how long, with whom, what it's like, what it involves.
**Q:** Where do you live?
**Direct Answer:** I live in a rented flat in the eastern part of the city, **Extension:** about ten minutes' walk from my office, which is the main reason we chose it.
**Q:** Do you work or study?
**Direct Answer:** I'm working at the moment - I'm a pharmacist at a hospital. **Extension:** I've been there just over three years now, mostly on the night shift.

**Strategy 2 - A.R.E: Answer – Reason – Example (3 steps)**
**When:** questions with a hidden "why" - Do you like...? Do you prefer...? Is ... important? Would you like to...? Most Part 1 questions follow this pattern.

**Step 1 - Answer:** a clear yes/no/it depends.

**Step 2 - Reason:** because / since / mainly because / the thing is.

**Step 3 - Example:** a concrete example or situation from your own life.
**Q:** Do you prefer tea or coffee?
**Answer:** Tea, without a doubt. **Reason:** Partly it's habit - I grew up in a house where the kettle was always on - but I also find coffee makes me jittery. **Example:** Last month I switched to coffee for a week to stay awake for exams and barely slept, so I went straight back to tea.
**Q:** Is it important to have a good relationship with your neighbours?
**Answer:** I think so, yes, especially in a city. **Reason:** Your family might be hundreds of kilometres away, and your neighbours are the only people close enough to help in an emergency. **Example:** When our electricity went out for a whole night last summer, the family upstairs lent us a lamp and kept our food in their fridge.

**Strategy 3 - L.D.F: Likes – Frequency – Reason (3 steps)**
**When:** questions about hobbies, free time, routines and habits - What do you do in your free time? Do you play any sport? How often do you...? With these questions, the listener wants to know both "what you do" and "how often".

**Step 1 - Likes:** what you like doing (use different verbs: I'm into, I'm keen on, I spend a lot of time...).

**Step 2 - Frequency:** how often and when (from the frequency list above).

**Step 3 - Reason:** why you enjoy it / what it gives you.
**Q:** What do you like doing at the weekend?
**Likes:** I'm quite into cycling these days. **Frequency:** I try to go out every Friday morning, usually for an hour or so before the roads get busy. **Reason:** It's the only time in the week when I'm not looking at a screen, and I come back with a much clearer head.
**Q:** Do you listen to music?
**Likes:** All the time - mostly old Bangla band songs, and some instrumental stuff when I'm working. **Frequency:** Pretty much daily; my commute alone is an hour of music. **Reason:** On a crowded bus it's the one thing that makes the journey bearable, and it puts me in a decent mood before I reach the office.

**Which one when - at a glance:** The question doesn't ask for a reason (what/where/how long) → **Direct Answer + Extension**. The question involves a preference, an opinion or a "why" → **A.R.E**. The question is about habits or free time → **L.D.F**. If in doubt, use A.R.E - it works everywhere.
If we break the three strategies down a little further, Part 1 questions fall into **7 types**. Next to each one is the strategy that works best for it.
Do you like...? / Are you interested in...? / Is ... important to you?
Clear yes/no (or "it depends") → reason → one detail. "Not really, to be honest. I find ... a bit ..., so I'd rather ..."
How often do you...? / Do you often...?
Frequency phrase → when/in what situation → why. "Maybe two or three times a month, usually at weekends when..."
Do you prefer A or B? / Which do you like more?
Preference → reason → exception. "I'd go for A most of the time, mainly because ... Having said that, when ..., B works better."
What's your ... like? / Tell me about ... / What kind of ... do you...?
General picture → 2 specific details → your feelings. "It's a fairly ... place. There's ... and ..., and I quite like the fact that ..."
Did you ... when you were a child? / Has ... changed?
Past (used to / past simple) → now (present) → reason/feeling. "When I was a kid I used to ..., but these days I ... , mostly because ..."
Would you like to ... in the future? / Will you ...?
Wish → condition → reason. "I'd love to, if I ever get the chance, because ..."
Do you think ... is important? / Why do people...?
Opinion → reason → your own example. "I think so, yes. It ..., and in my own case ..."
**Answer in the first sentence.** "Do you like cooking?" → your first word should be Yes/No/Sort of/It depends - no introduction.
**Don't hand the question's words back.** "Do you like cooking?" → "Yes, I like cooking" (weak) vs "Yes, I'm quite into it, actually" (good).
**Never stop at Yes/No.** Always add "because", "since", "the thing is".
**Keep your present tense accurate.** Most Part 1 questions are about habits - "I go", "she works", "it takes". Don't forget the third-person -s.
**Use degree adverbs instead of 'very':** quite, pretty, fairly, really, absolutely, a bit, not particularly.
**Give one concrete detail.** Compared with "I like music", "I like music - mostly old Bangla band songs from the nineties" gives the examiner far more language.
**Give the answer that gives you more to say.** Nobody checks whether it's true.
**One or two Part 3-style questions may come up** ("Why do you think people like ...?"). Don't panic; give a brief opinion, give a reason, and move on.
"How often" questions are very common in Part 1. Don't use only "sometimes" and "always" - add variety from the list below.
pretty much every day, almost daily, as a rule, without fail, whenever I get the chance
a couple of times a week, every other day, most weekends, fairly regularly, on a regular basis
now and then, from time to time, every so often, once in a while, occasionally
hardly ever, rarely, once in a blue moon, not as often as I'd like, only on special occasions
never, not at all, I've never actually..., it's just not something I do

Now for the topic bank. For each topic, ★★★ next to a question means it is very common in the test, ★★ means it comes up sometimes, and ★ means it comes up less often - but this categorisation is based on my own experience; any of them can come up in the test. After reading each model answer, **put in your own information** and say your own answer out loud - that's the practice.

chapters.title: How to Build Your Own Answers for Part 1
blocks: Reading the 130 answers above doesn't mean you're ready for Part 1. Apply the method below to all 32 topics - about 8-10 hours of work in total, and after that no Part 1 question will take you by surprise.

**Write down 3 true facts about yourself for each topic.** Work: where, how long, the best/worst thing about it. Food: your favourite food, whether you can cook, what you don't eat. These are your "raw material".
**Choose a precise word or collocation for each fact.** Not "I like my job" - but "I find it rewarding / it's fairly demanding / the hours are flexible".
**Using the 7 question patterns (above), say 3 answers out loud for each topic**, record them and listen back.
**Listen to the recording and look for three things:** where you say "umm", which words keep coming up, and which answers end after a single word. These are the areas to work on.

**A week later, speak on the same topic again - without looking.** If the main ideas come back but the words are a little different, you're on the right track. If exactly the same sentences come out, you've memorised them - and the examiner will notice.

**Final word:** The best Part 1 answer is one that sounds as if you're chatting with a friend at a tea stall - just in English, and a little more organised. The examiner doesn't want anything more than that.

chapters.title: Part 2: Cue Card - What Happens and What's Expected
blocks: At the end of Part 1, the examiner will say something like this: "Now I'm going to give you a topic, and I'd like you to talk about it for one to two minutes. Before you talk, you'll have one minute to think about what you're going to say. You can make some notes if you wish." Then they will give you a card, a piece of paper and a pencil. The card looks like this:

**Describe a skill you learned from an older person.**
You should say:

  what the skill is

  who taught you and when

  how you learned it

and explain how you feel about having this skill now.

Every card has the same structure: a **main topic** (the first line), three **bullet points** (hints about what to say), and at the end an **"and explain..."** - which always asks for your feelings, opinion or reasons. This last line is the most important and the most often ignored.
What the examiner is looking for here

Part 2 is the only part of the test where you speak **alone, continuously and without interruption**. In Part 1, the short questions help you; in Part 3, the examiner's questions give you direction. In Part 2, the direction is up to you. So here the examiner mainly looks at:
Can you keep talking for **up to 2 minutes**, or do you run out after 45 seconds?
Is your talk **going somewhere** - does it have a beginning, a middle and an end - or is it all over the place?
Can you **tell a story** - past tense, sequence, description, feelings?
Are you staying **on the topic**, or saying something else (something memorised)?
**Try to fill the full 2 minutes.** The examiner will stop you at 2 minutes - that's a good sign. If you stop before 1 minute, it directly hurts your FC score.
**Don't be upset if you're stopped.** "...and that's when I - " "Thank you." - that's the script. Being stopped midway means you had plenty to say.

**Use the full time for your 1-minute notes.** There's no benefit in saying "I'm ready" and starting early - in fact, it hurts you. 60 seconds of thinking now means 60 seconds less thinking during your 2-minute talk.

chapters.title: The 1-Minute Note: What to Write and What Not to Write
blocks: The biggest mistake in note-taking is **writing sentences**. In one minute you can write two sentences at most, and then you'll read those two sentences out - reading, not speaking. The examiner can tell the difference between reading and speaking in a second.
The second mistake is **writing nothing at all** - "I can keep it in my head". 90 seconds in, feeling nervous, you'll forget your third point.

Write **one keyword** for each of the card's four lines (three bullets + "explain"), plus **one extra** - something the card didn't ask for but that makes your story real. That's 5 words in total, in capital letters, written one below the other. For the card above, it could be:

SEWING - grandmother, Eid holidays, age 12

WATCH → PRACTISE → MISTAKES (crooked hem)

NOW: fix own clothes, save money

FEEL: proud, connected to her

+ old black machine, foot pedal sound

Notice: each line can be read at a glance, and you can get 2-3 sentences out of each word. The last line (+) is the "sensory detail" - a sight, sound or smell that makes the story feel true and gives you a chance to show your vocabulary.
Read the whole card - especially the last line. Choose **one** specific thing/person/event. Don't hesitate between two; take the first one that comes to mind, the one you have more to say about.
Say your first sentence in your head. If the start is right, the rest follows.

**Being truthful about the topic:** "Describe a skill you learned from an older person" - if you don't really have anything like this, make it up, or use something close (even if you learned it from a friend, say "my older cousin"). The examiner doesn't check whether it's true. But **don't change the topic** - talking about a journey instead of a skill is off-topic, and it hurts your FC score.

chapters.title: The 2-Minute Talk: Structure
blocks: This is Tip #3 - "Master Part 2 Structure". Any cue card, any topic: the same five steps. This is the only thing in this book you need to memorise - and once you've memorised it, you don't need to memorise anything else.
What you're going to talk about - in one sentence, paraphrasing the card's wording.
I'd like to talk about... / The [skill/place/person] I've chosen is... / OK, so this is about...
What, who, when, where - the background. Past tense here, and description of the person/place.
This was back when... / It all started... / She was the kind of person who...
How - step by step, a small incident, a problem and its solution. This is where the story is.
At first... then... / The tricky part was... / I remember one time...
The last line of the card. How you feel, why it matters, what has changed. Come back to the present tense.
Looking back, ... / What it means to me now is... / The reason it matters is...
Finish in one sentence - the future, or the main point again.
So, all in all... / That's why I'll always... / I suppose that's the story of...
Worked example: from note to talk
The full talk built from the note above. Each step is marked. It's about 2 minutes - 280-300 words at a natural pace.

**[1 Opening]** The skill I'd like to talk about is sewing, which I learned from my grandmother when I was about twelve.
**[2 Context]** This was during the long Eid holidays, when we'd go to stay at her house in the village for a couple of weeks. She had this ancient black sewing machine - the kind you work with a foot pedal - and I can still hear the rhythm of it, this steady clacking sound coming from the back room every afternoon. She was a very patient woman, but also quite strict about doing things properly, which turned out to be exactly what I needed.
**[3 Process]** At first she wouldn't let me touch the machine at all. For the first few days I just watched her, and then she gave me scraps of old cloth to practise straight lines on. The tricky part was keeping the pressure on the pedal steady - I remember my first hem came out completely crooked, and instead of fixing it for me, she made me unpick the whole thing and do it again. I was annoyed at the time, but by the end of the holiday I'd made a small cushion cover on my own.
**[4 Explain]** Looking back, I feel genuinely proud of having this skill, partly because so few people my age can do it. On a practical level, I fix my own clothes instead of throwing them away, which saves money and, honestly, feels quite satisfying. But more than that, every time I sit at a machine I feel connected to her - she passed away a few years ago, and this is the most tangible thing she left me.
**[5 Closing]** So I suppose it's much more than a skill to me; it's a bit of her that I still carry around.

What this talk contains that the examiner is looking for: past narrative (was, wouldn't let, came out, made me), sensory detail (black machine, clacking sound), a small problem and its solution (crooked hem), reflection in the present tense, precise vocabulary (ancient, steady, unpick, tangible), and a clear ending.

chapters.title: Strategies for Filling 2 Minutes
blocks: "I have nothing to say" - this is the most common complaint about Part 2, and it's almost always wrong. There are things to say; you just don't know which angle to look from. Apply the 6 "lenses" below to any topic, and 2 minutes will actually feel short.
When was the first time? What's it like now? What comes next?
First went there in 2nd year... now go every Thursday... will probably keep going after I graduate.
What does it look, sound, smell and taste like?
Dim yellow lights, smell of cardamom tea, old Bangla songs playing softly.
Who is there? Who do you go with?
The owner, who remembers everyone's order; my two closest friends.
How is it different from the others? What was there before?
Unlike the chain cafés, nobody hurries you out; before it opened, there was nowhere to sit near campus.
A small incident on one particular day?
The night we stayed until closing finishing a group project, and the owner brought us free tea.
What does it mean in your life? What has it changed?
It's where most of my university friendships were actually built.
The card's three bullets usually cover lenses 1, 3 and 5; the "explain" line is lens 6. The other two (senses, contrast) are your own additions - and they are what turn a Band 6 into a Band 7.
If you run out of things to say midway
**Look at your notes** - which keyword haven't you used yet? Go there: "Oh, and another thing I should mention is..."
**Switch lenses**: you've been describing what happened → now say how you feel about it. "Thinking about it now, ..."
**Make a comparison**: "Compared to other [cafés/gifts/journeys] I've had, this one..."
**Wrap it up** - once you've passed 1 minute 20 seconds, stopping neatly with a closing is better than forcing it to drag on.
The language of Part 2: a storytelling toolkit
back in [year], a few years ago, when I was in my final year, at the time, around that period, it must have been [season]
to begin with, after a while, the next thing I knew, eventually, by the end of it, in the end
she was the kind of person who..., he had a way of..., what struck me about her was..., a bit of a [perfectionist / joker]
tucked away behind..., it's the sort of place where..., what makes it special is..., nothing fancy, but...
I was over the moon, I was a nervous wreck, I couldn't believe my luck, I was a bit taken aback, it was a real eye-opener
looking back, in hindsight, thinking about it now, it still makes me smile, I'll always be grateful for
the thing I remember most vividly is..., what really stood out was..., I'll never forget...
Going through the card's bullets one by one with one sentence each ("The skill is sewing. My grandmother taught me. I learned by practising. I feel good.") - finished in 30 seconds.
Think of each bullet as a paragraph of 2-4 sentences. Use the lenses.
Speaking in general terms ("Sewing is a useful skill. Many people learn sewing...") - that's Part 3 language.
Part 2 is personal and specific: "I", "my", a particular person, day or place.
Giving a memorised talk that only partly matches the card.
The examiner will notice and ask different questions in the follow-up. Memorise the structure, not the content.
Using the present tense in a story about the past ("Then she gives me cloth and I practise...").
Write "PAST" next to your notes. If you start your first sentence in the past, the rest is easier.
Giving the whole talk while looking at your notes.
Notes are for a quick glance; 80% of the time, look at the examiner.
Leaving out the "Explain" line, or getting it over with in one sentence.
This is the 30-second part, and it's where the best vocabulary (feelings, reflection) comes in.

At the end of your talk, the examiner may ask one or two short questions: "Do you still sew?", "Would you teach this to someone?" These are not Part 3 - answer in **one or two sentences**. If you give a long answer, they will stop you.

chapters.title: Part 3: Discussion - The Game Changes
blocks: At the end of Part 2, the examiner takes the card back and says: "We've been talking about a skill you learned from an older person, and I'd like to discuss with you one or two more general questions related to this." Those words "more general" are what Part 3 is all about. The questions are no longer about you - they're about **people, society, the country and the future**.
Describe a skill you learned from an older person.

What kinds of skills do older people typically pass on to younger generations? / Are traditional skills disappearing in your country? Why? / Should schools teach practical skills like cooking or repairing things? / In the future, will people learn more from other people or from the internet?

This is Tip #5 - "Handle Part 3 Abstract Questions". In Part 3, the examiner wants to see whether you can **give opinions, explain reasons, compare, speculate and see both sides** - in other words, whether you can **think** in English. This is your biggest chance to show your range of vocabulary and grammar, and most Band 7 decisions are made here.
**"I have to give the right answer."** No. The examiner has no answer key. Whatever opinion you can explain best is the right one.

**"I have to know about the subject."** No. "I don't know much about this, but I'd guess..." - this is a perfectly acceptable start; then make a reasoned guess. Your language is assessed, not your knowledge.
**"Short answers, like in Part 1."** No. Part 3 answers are 4-6 sentences, 30-45 seconds. The examiner will stop you if they want to; don't stop on your own after two sentences.

chapters.title: 8 Types of Part 3 Questions
blocks: Like Part 2, Part 3 is predictable - not the topics, but the **question types**. Whatever the topic, the examiner asks these 8 types of question. If you can recognise each one, the language for your answer is already prepared.
Do you think...? Should...? Is it better to...?
I'd say / I tend to think / I'm inclined to believe / on balance
Why do people...? What makes...? Why is ... popular?
the main reason is / it's largely because / one factor is / this is partly down to
What effect does ... have on...? How does ... influence...?
this leads to / as a result / one consequence is / it tends to make people
How is ... different from...? Old vs young? City vs village?
whereas / while / unlike / on the one hand... on the other / far more likely to
Has ... changed? How was it different in the past?
used to / these days / there's been a shift towards / a generation ago
Will ... in the future? How might ... change?
I imagine / it's likely that / we may well see / I doubt whether / in the next decade or so
How can we...? What should the government do?
one option would be / the government could / a more effective approach might be / it would help if
Advantages/disadvantages? Is it a good thing?
the upside is / a major drawback / it cuts both ways / the benefits outweigh

chapters.title: A.R.E + Balance: The Framework for Part 3
blocks: The A.R.E from Parts A and B works here too - just with a fourth step added. In Part 3, the examiner wants to see whether you can see **more than one side** of an issue. So end your answer with a "but" - the other side, a condition, or an exception.

**A.R.E + B**
**A - Answer:** a clear opinion, in the first sentence. (A little more hedged than in Part 1: "I'd say", "generally")

**R - Reason:** why - one or two reasons, talking about people/society in general.

**E - Example:** a concrete example - your own country, someone you know, a trend.

**B - Balance:** "Having said that..." / "Of course, it depends..." / "That's not to say..." - the other side, in one or two sentences.

**Q:** Should schools teach practical skills like cooking or repairing things?
**A:** I think they should, yes - at least the basics.
**R:** The main reason is that these are skills everyone needs, regardless of what career they end up in, and a lot of families simply don't pass them on anymore because parents are working long hours.
**E:** In my country, for instance, plenty of university students can solve calculus problems but can't cook a meal or change a fuse, and they end up either dependent on others or spending money they don't have.
**B:** Having said that, I wouldn't want it to eat into academic time - maybe an hour a week would be enough, rather than a whole subject.

With these four steps, you show all of this in a single answer: opinion language, cause language, an example (a chance for LR), and contrast (GRA -'although', 'whereas', conditional). That's a Band 7 Part 3 answer.
Having said that, / Then again, / That said, / Mind you, / On the flip side,
It really depends on..., / As long as..., / Provided that..., / Unless...
That's not to say..., / Of course, there are exceptions - / This doesn't apply to everyone;
To some extent, / Up to a point, / In most cases, though not all,
I think the answer is somewhere in the middle. / It's probably a case of both. / The ideal would be a mix of...
Hedging: polite language for giving opinions

In Part 3, saying something like "Governments must ban cars" sounds immature. "I think governments should probably look at restricting cars in city centres" - the same opinion, but in the language of a thoughtful person. This hedging is essential for Band 7+:
People tend to be less active than they used to be.
It's quite likely to happen. / I'd expect that to happen.
Most people would probably agree that... / There's a general feeling that...
This can be problematic in some ways. / I'm not sure this is entirely a good thing.
The internet is arguably one of the main reasons. / I'd put a lot of it down to the internet.
When you don't know the answer
In Part 3 you will definitely get questions you've never thought about. When that happens, there are three routes - all acceptable; silence is not:
**Think and speculate:** "That's not something I've thought about, but I'd imagine... because..."
**Generalise from your own experience:** "I can only really speak from what I've seen in my own family, but there..."
**Narrow the question down:** "It probably depends a lot on the country. In mine, ..."
You can't just say "I don't know" to the examiner and stop - but you can say "I don't know, but..." and keep going.

chapters.title: Worked Example: A Full Part 3 on One Topic
blocks: Below is a full Part 3 arising from a Part 2 topic - 6 of the 8 question types, each answered with A.R.E + B. Notice the length of the answers: 4-6 sentences.
**The Part 2 topic was: Describe a journey you took by public transport that you remember well.**

Q1 (Reason): Why do some people prefer public transport to driving?
A: I'd say it comes down to cost and stress, mostly. Owning a car is enormously expensive once you add fuel, parking and repairs, whereas a bus or metro pass is a fraction of that. On top of that, in a congested city, sitting on a train reading is far less draining than sitting in traffic gripping a steering wheel. My cousin actually sold his car last year for exactly that reason. Of course, this only holds where public transport is decent - if the buses are unreliable, people will drive no matter the cost.
Q2 (Compare): How is travelling by public transport different in cities and in the countryside?
A: They're almost two different worlds. In cities, the issue is usually overcrowding - the transport exists, but there's too much demand for it, so rush hour is unpleasant. In rural areas, it's the opposite: services are so infrequent that missing one bus can mean waiting three hours. Where my grandparents live, there are two buses a day, so people plan their whole week around them. Having said that, rural journeys tend to be more pleasant when they do happen - you actually get a seat and a view.
Q3 (Past vs Now): Has public transport in your country changed in recent years?
A: Quite dramatically, at least in the capital. A generation ago it was entirely buses - old, crowded, with no fixed timetable. Now there's a metro line, and it's changed people's expectations: for the first time, a journey has a predictable length. That said, outside the capital things have moved much more slowly, so the gap between the big city and everywhere else has, if anything, widened.
Q4 (Solution): What could governments do to encourage more people to use public transport?
A: The most effective thing would probably be reliability rather than price. People will pay a reasonable fare if they know the bus will actually come. So investing in proper timetables, dedicated bus lanes and real-time tracking apps would do more than subsidies. Singapore is often cited as an example where this works. I'd add, though, that carrots alone aren't enough - some cities have only succeeded when they also made driving less convenient, through congestion charges or parking limits.
Q5 (Evaluate): What are the disadvantages of relying on public transport?
A: The obvious one is loss of control - you're tied to someone else's schedule and route, which is a real problem if you work irregular hours or have young children to carry around. There's also the comfort issue; a packed bus in forty-degree heat is nobody's idea of a good start to the day. And for people with mobility problems, a lot of systems simply aren't accessible. On balance, though, I'd argue these are problems of poor implementation rather than of public transport itself.
Q6 (Predict): How do you think people will travel around cities in fifty years?
A: I'd imagine private car ownership will have dropped sharply, at least in cities. Between shared electric vehicles, better rail and possibly self-driving shuttles, owning a car that sits parked ninety percent of the time will seem wasteful, the way owning a landline seems now. I'm less sure about the timeline - these things always take longer than the headlines suggest. And I doubt it'll happen evenly; wealthier cities will get there first, and places like mine might still be catching up.
Talking about yourself as in Part 1 ("I use the bus every day because...") when the question is about people in general.
Start with "People", "most families", "in my country"; use your own example only in the E step.
A.R.E + B - don't stop until you've gone through all four steps.
Only one opinion, only one side.
The Balance step is compulsory - it's where you show complex grammar.
Wasting time with "It's a good question", and then still giving an introduction.
One filler phrase, then straight to A.
Collapsing under the examiner's counter-argument (changing your opinion when you hear "But some people say...").
The examiner is testing whether you can hold your opinion. "That's a fair point, but I'd still say..." - keep your opinion and expand your language.

chapters.title: How to Practise Parts 2 and 3
blocks: **One cue card a day** (from Part D). 1 minute of notes - timer on your phone. 2 minutes of talk - recorded.
**Three questions when you listen to the recording:** Did you reach 2 minutes? Were all five steps there? Was your past tense correct?
**The Part 3 questions for the same card** (given with each card in Part D) - answer each one with A.R.E + B, 30-45 seconds.
**One full mock a week:** a friend or family member plays the examiner - Part 1 to Part 3, 12 minutes, recorded.
**After four weeks, listen to your first week's recording.** You'll hear the difference yourself - and that will be your source of confidence on test day.

chapters.title: The Week Before the Test: Checklist
blocks: The book is finished. Now come the last seven days of turning it into a score.
Reread the "10 Speaking Tips" in Part A. Listen to your oldest recording, then your newest - hear the difference. That is your confidence.
Part B: 10 random topics, 2 questions on each, using the three strategies. Record yourself and just count the 'umm's.
4 cue cards from Part D, from four different categories, timed. Answer each card's Part 3 questions with A.R.E + B.
Full mock: a friend as examiner, 12 minutes, Part 1→3, recorded. Listen back and compare yourself with the band descriptors in Part A.
Pronunciation day: pairs of difficult sounds, 10 minutes of shadowing, and one Part 2 talk purely for stress and intonation.
Second full mock, on different topics. Read the "10 mistakes Bangla speakers make" list in Part A out loud once.
**Nothing new.** Read the "Test day" chapter in Part A. Sort out your ID, the test centre address and your clothes. Have a relaxed 15-minute chat with someone in English. Go to bed early.

From one hour before, English only. Take three deep breaths before you enter the room. Make your first sentence clear, and say it with a smile. If you pause in an answer, pause in English. At the end, "Thank you". You know the rest.

**Final word:** The examiner is not against you. They are sitting there to hear you speak English for 11 minutes, and their job is to find out what you can do. Your job is simply to let them hear it. This book is here to make that easier. The rest - the preparation you have done - is yours.
